title: Wealth Tax Watch · Issue 01 · September 2026
description: Issue 01 of Wealth Tax Watch: California’s Proposition 40 polls, France’s Cour des comptes wealth levy, Canadian and UK proposals, and where BRICS, the G20 and the UN tax convention stand. September 1-23, 2026.
hero_lede: Wealth taxation is now on a ballot, in a public audit and in budget-season proposals. It is not yet in any international agreement, and nothing we track this issue has become law.

overview.title: A debate moving at different speeds

tracker.title: Everything we follow, and how far it has got
tracker.intro: Every development in this issue, placed on the road from research to enacted law. Tap a card to flip it for the short version. Filter by jurisdiction.
tracker.enacted_note: Nothing tracked in this issue has become law. The only machinery actually adopted is for cooperation, not taxation.

items.title: OECD Tax Policy Reforms 2026
items.summary: Covers 2025 reforms in 92 jurisdictions. Property taxes leaned towards raising revenue; changes to net wealth taxes stayed limited.

items.title: European Commission wealth-tax study
items.summary: Wealth taxes examined were not major revenue sources, largely because of reliefs, exemptions and weak compliance. No policy recommendation.

items.title: Tax Justice Network flows tracker
items.summary: About US$673 billion crosses European borders each year for tax abuse; about US$100 billion a year in tax is lost. A tax-abuse estimate, not wealth-tax revenue.

items.title: International Panel on Inequality
items.summary: Launched at UNGA by South Africa, Brazil, Norway and Spain. An evidence and coordination body modelled on the IPCC, not a tax instrument.

items.title: BRICS tax working groups
items.summary: Two new working groups on international taxation and transfer pricing, and on revenue statistics. Cooperation machinery, with no shared wealth tax.

items.title: UN tax convention talks
items.summary: Line-by-line negotiation of the framework convention and two early protocols began in New York. The protocols do not address wealth taxation.

items.title: CCPA annual wealth tax
items.summary: A progressive tax on net worth above C$10 million, estimated at more than C$39 billion in its first year. Not federal policy.

items.title: CCPA inheritance tax
items.summary: A 50% tax on lifetime inheritances above C$2.5 million, about C$1.1 billion a year, alongside a 37% bracket above C$1 million.

items.title: 2% tax on net assets above £10m
items.summary: Up to £24 billion a year, per Tax Justice UK. Collected in Compass’s 70-option menu; backed by a petition and a “Proud to Pay” letter.

items.title: 2% minimum tax above £100m
items.summary: Households worth over £100 million pay at least 2% of wealth in total personal taxes. About £10.4 billion in 2026 from fewer than 1,000 households; ten-year exit rule.

items.title: 0.7% tax on property value
items.summary: Replace Council Tax and Stamp Duty on primary homes with a revenue-neutral 0.7% annual tax on current value. A property tax reform, not a net wealth tax.

items.title: The Zucman tax, again
items.summary: A 2% minimum tax on fortunes above €100 million, rejected by the Assemblée 228 to 172 in October 2025, now back in the Socialists’ alternative budget.

items.title: Cour des comptes package
items.summary: A differential charge on non-business wealth, a stronger holding-company tax and narrower Pacte Dutreil relief, offset by cuts in transfer duties and inheritance tax.

items.title: Proposition 40
items.summary: A one-time 5% tax on billionaires resident on January 1, 2026, mostly for health care. Polls range from 45% to 52% yes.

items.title: Propositions 41 and 42
items.summary: Rival measures backed by a Brin-funded group. If either passes with more yes votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire tax could be voided.

lead.title: A narrowing lead, and a ballot catch
lead.lede: A one-time 5% tax on billionaires faces three polls, two rival measures and more than $187 million in opposition money.

polls.title: Yes against no, three surveys
polls.sub: Percentage of respondents. Different methods and populations: compare within a row, not across rows.
polls.note: IGS polled online in English and Spanish and found a sharp partisan split: about 70% of Democrats in favour and 80% of Republicans opposed.

trend.title: The one like-for-like trend
trend.sub: Citrin Center / Politico, same pollster, February vs September.
trend.caption: Support down 5 points, opposition up 15. The gap shrank from 22 points to 2.

compare.title: If 41 or 42 beats 40, the billionaire tax could be voided
compare.text: Same survey (PPIC, likely voters), so these bars compare directly. Proposition 41 would nullify new state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that sit outside the spending limit; Proposition 42 would bar new state taxes on personal property. Both are backed by a group funded largely by Sergey Brin. Governor Newsom opposes Proposition 40.

numbers.title: Six figures, six different kinds of claim
numbers.intro: Each number is tagged by what it is. A poll is not a costing, and an advocacy estimate is not an official score. None of them add up.

dispatches.title: The full stories
dispatches.intro: Each dispatch is labelled by what it is: a ballot measure, a proposal, research, an audit or diplomacy.

discussion.title: Four designs. The same three problems.

designs.title: California’s one-time levy
answers: Billionaires’ net worth, once, at 5%. Most revenue goes to health care.
Residency is fixed in the past: anyone resident on January 1, 2026 owes it, so leaving now does not help.
The Legislative Analyst sees “tens of billions” over several years, plus a possible ongoing income-tax loss if billionaires leave. The sponsor’s ~$100bn is a campaign figure.

designs.title: UK minimum tax
answers: Households above £100 million must pay at least 2% of wealth a year in total personal taxes; taxes already paid count towards it.
A ten-year post-emigration liability: people stay liable for a decade after leaving.
About £10.4bn in 2026 from fewer than 1,000 households, after avoidance and behavioural responses. A research estimate.

designs.title: France’s differential charge
answers: Non-business wealth only, alongside the real-estate wealth tax. Business assets stay out.
Stronger taxation of personal holding companies and narrower Pacte Dutreil relief close common routes around the tax.
€1.83bn net after the package’s own tax cuts. An official audit, not a government bill.

designs.title: Canada’s holdings plus inheritance
answers: An annual progressive tax on net worth above C$10 million, plus a 50% tax on lifetime inheritances above C$2.5 million.
Paired with C$2 billion over three years for CRA enforcement, against planned CRA job cuts.
More than C$39bn in year one, an advocacy costing built on Oxfam Canada modelling, not a PBO or Finance Canada score.

discussion.question: Which design choice would survive in your own jurisdiction, and which assumption would fail first?
